title: Short Stuff: NYT Bestseller List
summary: Short Stuff episode on the New York Times Bestseller List. Josh and Chuck, who note they are New York Times bestselling authors themselves (four weeks on the list), explain how the list works: eleven weekly and seven monthly lists, divided into fiction, nonfiction, children's categories and subcategories. They discuss the Times' claim that the list is independent of editorial, advertising and business pressure and is based on confidential data from booksellers, while industry skeptics doubt they avoid data aggregators. They cover ways authors game the list, including pre-order campaigns, giveaways tied to speaking engagements, and bulk purchases through companies like Book Highlight. The Times marks bulk-purchased titles with a dagger, which critics say still legitimizes the sales; examples include books bought by the RNC and a pro-Trump PAC, and CEO-authored books such as Howard Schultz's. Sophie Verschbau's Esquire article is cited as a source.
topics: how the NYT bestseller list works

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the NYT list
segments.summary: Hosts joke about being New York Times bestselling authors after four weeks on the list, then introduce the list as the industry standard for measuring book sales and cite the Esquire article by Sophie Verschbau.

segments.title: How the list is structured
segments.summary: The list has eleven weekly and seven monthly lists, split into fiction, nonfiction and children's books, with subcategories such as hardcover, paperback, how-to, middle grade, picture books, and young adult.

segments.title: Mass market paperbacks
segments.summary: Josh explains mass market paperbacks as cheaply printed books distributed like magazines, often sold in airport spinner racks.

segments.title: Data sources and the Times' methodology claims
segments.summary: The Times says it uses confidential data from thousands of retailers, weighted differently, and denies using data aggregators. Industry insiders doubt this, and the hosts note the methodology is published but the exact formula is not, so raw sales data does not fully explain rankings.

segments.title: Leaks and secrecy at the bestseller desk
segments.summary: Josh jokingly says the bestseller desk is tightly guarded against leaks.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Break before the discussion of gaming the system.

segments.title: Pre-orders, giveaways and speaking events
segments.summary: Legitimate ways to tip the list include pre-orders, which roll into week-one sales, plus giveaways and books bundled with speaking engagements. The hosts say they pre-ordered and stayed on the list for four weeks.

segments.title: Book Highlight and bulk buying
segments.summary: Companies such as Book Highlight reportedly let authors buy large numbers of their own books through independent booksellers in small batches to look like organic sales, a practice described as book laundering.

segments.title: The dagger mark for bulk purchases
segments.summary: The Times tracks bulk purchases and marks such titles with a dagger rather than excluding them. Critics say listing them legitimizes the purchases, and the hosts note that most readers treat daggered books as simply bestsellers.

segments.title: Daggered books: business authors and political buyers
segments.summary: Health, self-help, diet and CEO-written books are cited as frequent daggered titles. Examples include Donald Trump Jr., whose book was bought by the RNC for $100,000 in week one, Jared Kushner, whose book was bought by a pro-Trump PAC for $158,000, and Howard Schultz of Starbucks. Josh says the criticism is that daggered authors are rewarded while genuine authors are left off.

segments.title: Closing banter and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts joke that they did not game the list, thank readers who bought their book, and sign off.

segments.title: Production credit and podcast promotion
segments.summary: Closing credit noting the show is an iHeartRadio production and promoting other podcasts.
